clean.title: Clear cache
clean.confirm:
Clearing the cache is rarely needed.

Cached (standby) memory is not wasted RAM: Windows hands it to any program that asks, instantly. After clearing, programs and files have to be read from disk again, so the PC may feel slower for a while.

Clear it anyway?
clean.failed: The cache could not be cleared. This needs administrator rights; see the log.
tip.available: Memory programs can get right away: free + cached. This is the number to watch.
tip.cached: Same value as "Cached" in Task Manager: standby + modified pages. It is not wasted RAM; it makes programs open faster.
tip.standby: Copies of recently used files and programs kept in RAM. When a program needs memory, Windows releases it instantly. It is not wasted RAM; it makes programs open faster.
tip.free: Memory doing nothing at all. Windows prefers to use it as cache, so a low value is normal.
tip.modified: Pages whose contents changed and are waiting to be written to disk. After that they become cache.
tip.commit: Total memory reserved by programs (RAM + page file) and its limit. Near the limit, programs may fail with out-of-memory errors.
tip.inUse: Memory currently used by programs, drivers and Windows.
tip.clean: Empties the cache. Rarely needed; click for details.
info.title: How to read RAM
info.short: Cached memory is not wasted. Windows fills spare RAM with recently used files so programs open faster. What matters is the "Available" value.
info.long:
Available
Memory programs can get right away (free + cached). This is what tells you whether the PC will slow down.

Cached
Copies of recently used files and programs (standby + modified pages), the same as "Cached" in Task Manager. Windows hands the standby part to any program that asks, instantly. A large value is good.

Free
Memory doing nothing. Windows uses free memory as cache, so it naturally shrinks over time.

Modified
Pages waiting to be written to disk.

Commit
Total memory reserved by programs and its limit. Getting close to the limit is a real memory shortage.

When to worry?
When available memory stays below a few GB, or commit approaches its limit. The fix then is not clearing the cache, but closing the programs using the most RAM, or adding RAM.

details.title: {0} · details
details.gone: This program is no longer running.
details.noAccess: not readable (protected process or needs administrator rights)
details.sys.kind: A process of the Windows kernel itself: it has no program file or command line, and nobody, administrators included, can look inside it.
details.sys.compression: Memory Compression is Windows' compressed memory store. When RAM starts to fill up, pages that have not been used for a while are compressed and kept here instead of being written to disk; when a program needs them again they are unpacked right away. This is much faster than reading from disk. A large size is not a problem: it holds more data than the size shown.
details.sys.system: System is the process in which the Windows kernel and drivers run. It is not a real program and cannot be closed.
details.sys.registry: Registry is the in-memory copy of the Windows registry, kept here so that reading the registry does not go to disk every time. It cannot be closed.
details.sys.secure: Secure System is Windows' virtualization-based security (VBS) area. Sensitive data such as sign-in credentials is kept here, isolated from the rest of Windows, which is why it cannot be inspected - by design.
details.sys.idle: Idle (System Idle Process) is a placeholder that runs when the processor has nothing to do. It is not a real program.
details.sys.vmmem: vmmem is the memory used by WSL or Hyper-V virtual machines. The RAM of the programs running inside the virtual machine shows up here. It is given back to Windows when the virtual machine shuts down (for WSL: wsl --shutdown).

tip.critical: Below this much available RAM the icon turns red and you get a notification.
tip.warning: Below this much available RAM the icon turns amber.
tip.interval: How often memory is measured in the background.
tip.autoClean: Clears the cache at the critical threshold. It barely raises available memory; the program list in the notification is what really helps. Needs administrator rights: works when "Start with Windows" is on.
tip.startup: MemoryPulse starts in the notification area when you sign in. Asks for administrator permission once, so automatic cleaning works without a prompt every time.
settings.startupDisabledByUser: "Start with Windows" was turned off in Task Manager, so only you can turn it back on there: Task Manager > Startup apps > MemoryPulse > Enable.
tip.startupStore: MemoryPulse starts in the notification area when you sign in. You can also turn this off in Task Manager > Startup apps.

history.ioNote: Read/write (I/O): Windows counts file, network and device operations together in this number. The Received and Sent (network) columns are filled only for programs you right-clicked in the main list and chose "Watch network usage" for. Click a column header to sort.
history.ioTip: The Windows I/O (input/output) counters count everything a program reads and writes: files, network connections and devices. So it is not disk use alone. The programs using the most RAM or I/O at each moment are recorded; the average is over the moments the program was recorded.
history.eventsNote: This list is read from Windows' own event log; MemoryPulse does not record these itself. They also appear as dashed vertical lines on the charts.

history.watchNet.needsAdmin:
Measuring network use per program needs administrator rights.

Turn on "Start with Windows" in the settings (it asks once, then MemoryPulse starts with the permission every time), or close MemoryPulse and open it with "Run as administrator".

The network use of the whole computer is recorded without the permission too.
